headline: Exact Ramsey numbers for a cycle versus a clique: R(C_m, K_n) = (m − 1)(n − 1) + 1 when m ≥ n ≥ 3.
scope: Holds for all whole numbers m ≥ n ≥ 3 except m = n = 3, where the answer is 6.
plain: Colour every line between N points red or blue. How large must N be to force either a red loop through exactly m points or a blue group of n points all joined? Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp conjectured the answer (m − 1)(n − 1) + 1 in 1978. This paper proves it for every m ≥ n ≥ 3, apart from the known exception m = n = 3.
doesNot: This does not cover cycles shorter than the clique size, where m is less than n.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.significanceWhy: It settles a 1978 conjecture of Erdős and coauthors in its full stated range.

explanation:
Take six people and draw a line between every pair. Colour each line red or blue. Split the six into two groups of three. Colour lines inside each group red and lines between groups blue. Then no four people form a red loop, since each red cluster has only three people. And no three people are joined all in blue, since any three include two from the same group.

Add a seventh person, and this escape is gone. Whatever colours you choose, you get a red loop through exactly four people or a blue triangle. The paper's formula gives exactly that seven. In the language of the subject, R(C₄, K₃) = 7.

Here is the general setting. Join N points in every possible way and colour each line red or blue. A cycle C_m is a loop through exactly m points. A clique K_n is a set of n points all joined to each other. The Ramsey number R(C_m, K_n) is the smallest N that always forces a red C_m or a blue K_n[1].

In 1978, Erdős, Faudree, Rousseau and Schelp conjectured a formula. For m at least n at least 3, the answer should be (m − 1)(n − 1) + 1. The only exception is R(C₃, K₃) = 6. A red five-sided loop, with blue diagonals, shows why five points are not enough there. The lower bound comes from the opening picture, scaled up: n − 1 red clusters of m − 1 points, with blue lines between[3].

Many cases were settled one by one. The case n = 3 goes back to Chartrand and Schuster[4]. Bondy and Erdős handled very long cycles, and later work completed the cases n = 4 through 7[5]. In 2021, Keevash, Long and Skokan proved the formula for all large enough n. That left at most finitely many pairs open[6].

This paper proves the conjecture in full[2]. It does not need the size of the unknown constant from the 2021 result. It studies a smallest failing case and first finds a large clique inside it[7]. Then it grows paths between clique points and shows that certain improvements would close a loop of exactly the right length. The last small cases come down to 3,099 finite patterns across 42 parameter pairs[8]. A computer rules them out using proved rules. It searches patterns, not graphs or colourings[9]. Two separate programs do this, with full records of each deduction[10].

The difficulty is that the cycle length is exact[11]. A loop through more or fewer than m points does not count. That is why the paper tracks paths so carefully.

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has checked a formal version of the theorem. The Lean scope note says it covers every m at least n at least 3, plus the exception R(C₃, K₃) = 6. That is the paper's full range. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds. Lean has checked the full theorem; part of the paper's own proof uses computer checks of finite patterns, and no specialist review is published.
